MORE NEUTRALITY.
(From the Warrington Examiner.)

Ora epicene friend, the Warrington Guardian, sometimes escapes from the monotony of its own neutral tastes, by inviting into its columns the contributions of a gentleman who signs himself "Mercator," and who is always an able, ifamsuccessful, apologist of the present Government. When a paper has no reputation for consistency to support, it is an ingenious idea to select its leading articles in this manner, with .the graceful acknowledgement of aprending the corres- pondent's nom de plume at the foot. By this system, while the newspaper proprietor saves the money which he would otherwise have to pay for literary work, the writer has the advantage of propagating his Conserva- tive opinions. It is always desirable that independent thinkers should express them- selves through the medium of the press, and every section of the press. The character of a newspaper is in no way impeached by the insertion of outside communications ex- pressing contradictory sentiments. But when a journal profess ng strict neutrality in poli- tics, boasting every week of its own vacuity in all affairs temporal and sacred, permits the alteration of the epistslary form of a communication from a vehement political partisan, and prints it in its leadingcolumns, we are bound to suppose that although it has made no formal proclamation of its apostacy from political nothingness, and has not yet taken down the old sign-board, yet that it has discovered the mental malady of which neutrality was the symptom: that its political neutrslity hasripen ed at last into the seed of ultra-Tory convictions. The Eastern Question is not only the question of the day, but it is the only question of the day. In every company you enter, in every news- paper you consult, nothing else is discoursed. Yet most of that which you hear and read, is a hollow repetition of sentiment and opini n, based upon very imperfect know- ledge of the question. In the midst of his declamation, ask a man what was the origin of the insurrection and why Servia declared war, and in few cases will you elicit a cor- rect or even an intelligent reply. In the midst of his sonorous and skilful platitudes about homogeneous populations And his " in- finite deal of nothing" about autonomy, if we could arrest " Mercator" and ask him if he could throw any light upon the foreign policy of the Ministers after his own heart, should we be wiser than we are n w? How- ever, allowance must be made for a news- paper which has so recently embraced a political creed. Before it has mastered the catechism it would be wiser to abstain from polemics " Mercator" may be admirable on such subjects as "Church and State," or " Hereditary Legislators," but on the Eastern Question he is almost as indefinite as Lord Be csnsfield himself. Lord Derby addressing deputations in London with the masterly candenr which reveals nothing ex- cept the perverse resolution of the Cabinet to defy the people; Sir Stafford Northeote defending at Wakefield with hysterical yet melancholy sprightliness the despotism of himself and colleagues, which they natu- rally mistake for constitutional government, are interesting enough in their way, but we prefer to listen to the master spirit of Ayles- bury, who is the real " Dr. Slade" of the new Conservative spiritualism. '1 he Prime Minister at Aylesbury, with that jaunty style which the elderly l'ritish nobleman in- variably affects on the stage, and in the novel, took all his friends into his confidence and told them (as our readers will remoras ber)--nothing. The scene was one which must have excited even the oriental imagi- nation of the Premier. The honoured guest of his late constituents; an audience pre- ferred to laugh and cheer and open their bucolic eyes to receive the rhetorical dust with which Lord Beaconsfield delights to play; himself in an entirely new character in which he had once more the opportunity of displaying his versatility, and you have the crcumstences under which a manifesto was delivered, clever nly because it reveals no- thing that we did not know before. In other respects perhaps the speech was the most 111-advised, incautious, and defiant ever ad- dressed by the Prime Minister of a free people to a nation inflamed with that "sub- lime sentiment " which, he told us, was the finest force a Ministry could possess, but whether as an impelling force, or an expel- ling force, he did not say. For the benefit of what Lord Beaconsfield terms "coffee- house babblers," let us glance once more at the outline of this s rim and ghastly political landscape. 'Ye rs ago, with the pistol at his head, the Turk was compelled to grant self-government to her European and Chris- tian subjects. She was permitted to continue to levy a small contribution from these states, but so small that it can only have been valued as a token of fealty. Owing to the oppressive manner in which this tax, small as it was, was levied, the Bulgarians revoAed and the atrocities followed. It was then that Servia, sympathising with her fel- low Christians and fellow autonomists, joined the insurrection and declared war. We do know enough of the grievances of the people of Bulgaria to believe they are justified in rebelling, and we know a great deal .too nau&l of the devilish cruelties of the Circas- eian hordes, to feel ashamed that our Am• - bassador at Constantinople should have looked on with folded arms. These being the broad facts of the case, Lord Beacons- field talks of "this outrageous and wicked war" for, he continues, "of all the wars that ever took place there was never a war less justified than that between Servia and Tur- key." We have never had reason to charge Lord Beaconsfield with being without the "historic conscience" of which he is the in- ventor and patentee. he is simply the chartered libertine of debate. It is therefore not for hie sake, but for that of his less in- formed audience that we state that numbers of wars, entered upon under conditions almost identical with those of the present war, have been a great deal less justified. Why, look at our own country 250 years ago. At that time Scotland was as much an autonomous state paying tribute.to England as Servia is now. What took place? The English revolted against their Sultan, Charles 1., and our auts nomous friends crossed the border, came to our assistance' and helped us to behead that weak and foolish tyrant. Look at Poland; look at episodes in the American civil war; look at the war of Independence; look at each and every war of rebellion, ani find one which was as much justified as the present war, for to do so you will have to find one which has been provoked by the same oppression, the same cruelty, the same corruption. A.nd then Lord Beaconsfield " ungrateful" subjects of speaks of these the Sultan. What have they to be grateful for? Grateful because, at the dagger's point, he removed his corrupt executive and let them govern themselves? Grateful for exercising the only form of oppression left to him to exercise, and following it up with the burning of villages, the sacrilege of churches, and the violation of women? And then the farmers of Bucks cheered, and then they laughed, and the speech goes forth, and the dazed " coffee house babblers," and the " Mereators " of journalism speak of it with admiration, and are deaf and blind to the covert defiance which it casts at the "sub- lime sentiment" of the English people. This is the graver part of Lord Beacons- field's insolent and heart'ess blunder. By the side of it, we may almost afford to smile at the audacity with which he invented and introduced the secret societies as the myste- lions, unseen, but irrtsistable, element of oonflagration, Whcso gr 9 )115 V79*

" Servia declared war upon the Turks— that is to say the secret societies of Europe, through Servia, declared war on Turkey. I tell you, gentlemen, that in the attempt to conduct the government of this world there are new elements to be considered which. our predecessors had not to deal with. We have not only to deal w:th. Emperors and Princes and Ministers, but societies form an element we must take into consideration, which at the last moment may baffle all your arrangements, which have agents everywhere, which have reckless agents, which countenance assassination, and which, if necessary, can produce a massacre." In the pages of "Lothair" we were initiated into the mysteries of a secret society called "Mary Anne." but so far from being powerful and promoting massacres, it only got everbody connected with it into a scrape. The secret societies which were impotent and contemptible in the pages of his own romance, became formidable and omnipotent in the real life of the Prime Minister of Eng- land.

_ And now we must leave for a time both "Mercator" and Lord Beaconsfield. We shall always read with mingled feelings the special pleading of so clever a man as "Mer- cator." His eloquent yet dismal cynicism is not perhaps altogether new for the arch cynic of journalism—the "Saturday "—has long since familiarised us with the Mephis- tophelian philosophy, which teaches that there is "nothing new and nothing true, and it doesn't matter." As to Lord Beacons- field's speech, it does not candidly recognise the facts of the case; it does not cope with the definite charges brought against the Hovernment, it contains no pledge of a policy which would place us on a proper footing in Europe; it offers no effectual guarantee against the recurrence of abominable deeds which, though perpetrated upon "ungrate- ful subjects," have sent a shudder even through nations not altogether ignorant of milder forms of tyranny at home—tyranny which, at any rate, never degenerated into something utterly inhuman,

At the Lancaster county petty sessions, on Saturday Edwin Burrell, a provision dealer, of Morecambe, wa' charged with selling bread otherwise than by weight. Superintendent Jervis stated that he visited defendants shop and asked for a quartern loaf. Ho replied that he did not know what he meant, and in answer to another question, said he did not sell by weight. He tun asked for one of his largest loaves, and was sup- p ied with a sixpenny loaf. Compared with the price per lb. of bread at Lancaster, the loaf was 12L a. short of weight; and Dr. Brown, of Liverpool, to whom the IJaf had been sent for analysis, had informed the superintendent that it was litb. short according to the prevailing price there. Early planting is over the beat, Hand-setting, too, is a.first-class way of planting where labourers are plentiful; enough seed being saved to pay for the labour. Colin—Although there has been no general advance in prices this month, there is a stiffer tone in the ma-ket so far as the better classes of round coal are concerned, and colliery proprietors as a rule are not at all anxious sellers for forward delivery at present prices. For house-11re coal in the Manchester district an advance of 10d. per ton has keen made in some quarters, but no alteration has been made in the pit prices. The better classes of round coal in the Tvldesley district are also stiffer. In the Wigan and 'West Lancashire districts advances of 6d. and ls, per ton are being asked in some quarters on Pemberton fur-feet and best Arley classes of coal, but there Is no general upward movement in values; and although sellers are firm at late rates higher prices are (Moult to obtain, and the average pit quotations remain -about tlOs. to lb. per ton for good Arley, 9s. for Pemberton ;four-feet, and 6s. 6d. to 7s. 6d. and Bs. per ton for common coal. In other descriptions of coal there is no material change except that engine classes of fuel are rather more plentiful and easier in prices. For coke the demand continues to improve and some of the makers are now busy.

Irmy.—There is a stiffer tone in the iron trade of this district, and for north country brands of iron espeoially offering here more money is being asked by makers. In Lancashire pig iron there has been rather mare doing, and prices are firm at about late rate, No. 3 foundry delivered into the Manchester district being quoted at 565. to 57e. per ton and No. 4 forge 665. per ton. div.p: IMPORTANT GAS CASE AT ALTRINCHAM.

The Altrincham Gas Company broueht an action against George Smith, a gentleman residing at Tim- perley Lodge, Timperley, at the Altrincham County Couit, on Wednesday, to recover the sum of £3O odd, being the amount of a gas account owing by the des fendant, for gas supplied by the plaintiffs at his resi- dence. Mr. Harris appeared for the plaintiff d. The defendant had paid £22 into court, The defendant had declined to pay the account, stating as his reason that the meter registered more gas than was consumed, Ildr. Harris said that as the meter was Mr. Smith's pro- , Party he would be unable to get beyond that. If the Meter belonged to the company, he, the defendant, could have had it tested. The Judge; He tiny show that the quantity registered by the meter was more than was really the Case, The Act of Parliament empowers the Undertakers to remove a meter if they suspect it is in Improper order, but if it is found correct it is removed at their expense, but if incorrect at the expense of the Consumer. From the evidence it appeared that at the Periodical visits of the Inspector of the Gas Company, the defendant comPlsined of the excessive quantity of gas registred by the meter, and ultimately the Gas Company took out the meter, which was found to be egiAering 16 per cent, more than the actual consump. tion. The defendant refused to pay the accouut, and eventually the Company offered to make a deduction Of £3, which the defendant alleged was not sufficient, and declined to pay the account on those terms. The defendant stated that he wanted the meter tested by the Government Inspector in Manchester, but the plaintiffs would not permit hide to remove it. The iJudge said that in the absence of any evidence by the defendant as to the inacuracy of the meter, he must take it that that was prima facia evidence that it was tight. A verdict was given for the plaintiffs for the Amount claimed leas £3.

div.head: ALTRINCHAAI FORTY YEAES AGO.
div.p: ALTRINCHAAI FORTY YEAES AGO.

The inabitants of Altrincham and Bowdon, will probably be greatly amused and interested with a de- scription of Altrincham as it was forty years ago. The growth of Altrincham and Bowdon since that time has been of so extensive a character, that few people will recognise Altrincham under the description which was given it in owls' Topographical Dictionary of Eng- land, published forty-one years ago. In it Altrincham is thus described. A market town and chapelry in the parish of Bowdon, hundred of Bncklow, county pala- tine of Chester, containing 2,302 inhabitants. The town is situate on Bowdon Downs, and though small, contains several respectable dwelling-houses, the ealubrity of the air rendering it a place of general resort for invalids from Manchester, it is watched and lighted by subscription, and characterised throughout by cleanliness and neatness. The principift trade con- sists in the spinning of yarn, the making of bobbins for cotton and worsted spinners and in the weaving of cotton by hand-looms, for the manufacturers of Man- cl,eaer and other adjacent towns. The Duke of Bridgewater's canal from Manchester to Runcorn, passes through the town, and affords a facility for the conveyance of coal; early potatoes are cultivated here to a great extent for the Manchester market. The market days are Tuesday and Saturday, the latter being only for butcher's meat ; the fairs chiefly for the sale of live stock, are held on April 29th, August sth. and November 22, to the two last are attached courts if pie powder. Altrincham was made a free borough in the reign of Edward I, by a charter of Hamon de Massey, lord of the barony of Dunham Massey, whereby the burgesses were empowered to have a gild naerchant, and to choose a prepositus or bailiff; but the only privilege they now possess, is that of electing a mayor, at a court led held in autumn, when a jury of bur- gesses present three of their own body to the steward, who appoints one to the office, which is merely nominal, and the duty of which extends only to the opening of the fairs, the town being wholly within the jnrisdictien of the county magistrates. Pleas were formerly held in the lord's court, but have of late been discontinued. The living is a perpetual curacy in the archdeaconry and diocese of Chester, endowed with £lOOO parliamentary grant. The Earl of Stsmford and Warrington was patron in 1820. The chapal dedicated to St. George, is a plain brick building, erected by subscription in 1799. There are two places of worship for Methodists, and one for Unitarians. The Jubilee school built in 1810, is supported by subscription.

THE LATE COLLISION ON THE ALTRINCLIAM RAILWAY. Colonel Hutchinson, R.E„ has reported to the Board of Trade the result of his inquiry into the circular- *lances connected with the collision on the 12th August at Altrincham Junction, on the Manchester South Junction and Altrinchare Railway. It will be remem- bered that on the day in question the 11 p.m. Man- chester South Junction and Altriucham Company's down passenger train from Oxford Road Station, Manchester, to Bowdon, was run into by the 11.25 p.m. Cheshire Lines Committee up passenger train from Knntsford to Altrincleane. Three complaints of slight injury were made by passengers in the former train, but none front the passengers (there eras only one) in the latter. No companies' servants were in- jured. After giving the eviJence laid before him, Col. Hutchinson says The primary cause of this collision was want of reasonable caution on the part of the driver of the Kuuteford train in approaching Altriucham junction. He was no stranger on the line, and being aware of the relative positions of the back light of the Peel Cause- way down distant signal and the front light of the junction up home signal, and of the possibility of mis- taking one for the other, he should have been all the more careful to have made sure that the up junction signal was really lowered for him. But for the gross irregularity he had committed in allowing two un- authorised persons to travel on his engine to and from Knutsford, I should have been inclined to have paid more attention to his excuse, but under the circum- stances I think it highly probable that no proper look out was being kept on the engine, and that no attempt was made to stop until the Junction Company's train was seen crossing the junction, when it was too late to stop even the light train (consisting of only two vehicles besides the engine end tender) in time to avoid the collision. The guard also is much to blame for allowing three unauthorised persons to travel in his van, and I think ft very doubtful whether he kept the good look out and applied his brake in the way he describes. If his evidence is to be at all relied on, it contradicts that of the driver and fireman as to the back light of the Peel Causeway down distant signal, which they say was a green light, end he affirms was a white one, that of the junction up home signal being green. As the block system has since the collision been introduced between Altrinehana Junction and Peel Causeway, according to one of the rules for working which no two trains which can come into collision should be allowed to approach the j auction simultaneously, no similar collision to the present can recur so long as this rule is obeyed. It, how ever, transpired on the inquiry that the rule in question had, without any inetructione to that effect from the super- intendent of the line, not been acted on. The inquiry has thus brought to light several serious irregulari- ties, to obviate the 'recurrence of which the com- panies concerned ehould give the-r best attention. It is, no doubt, desirable to make an alteration in the height of the Peel Causeway down distant signal, so as to prevent the possibility of its back light being mistaken for that of the j auction up home

Joseph Tickle, beerhouse keeper, at Halton, was summoned for permitting drunkenness on his premises on the 17th ult, Mr. Beasley defended. Superintendent z,teen said the prosecution arose from some facts which were stated at an inquest last week, when it was proved that a woman named kiindley upon whom the inquest was held, had been seen drinking at the de- fendant's house, and was afterwards found drowned in the canal. From the evidence of George Dutton, it appeared that the deceased woman was seen in the defendant's house' and that she drank several glasses of ale, having had three glasses of whisky previously. When she left the house she was seen to fall, and was not again seen alive. Other persons who were with her, were also seen in a state of intoxication, and the result was that the deceased was found drowned in the canal. For the defence it was admitted that the de- ceased had been in his house, but that he did not ob- serve that she was drunk. It was argued that she might have obtained her drink elsewhere. The bench however, considered the ease proved, and indicted a fine of £2, and £2 6s. costs, or two months iropzison- ment. As the house bore a good character, the license was not endorsed.

div.p: A WOMAN DROWNED AT NORTIIWIOII.

An inquest was held at the Navigation Inn, Northd wich, before Mr. Dunstan, coroner, on the body of Sarah Ogden. Deceased had been cohabiting for some years with James Bobbing, a canal boatman. Lest Tuesday night Bebbing'a boat arrived at Northwich on Its way to Lancashire, and was moored near another boat belonging to Alexander Tyrer, of Bedford Leigh, in the river Weaver, a few yards from the Navigation Inn, Northwich. Deceased left the boat and went to the theatre, but came out with a ticket before the play was over. She went to the Navigation Inn and asked for a glass of beer, but the landlady refused to let her have it. Tyrer's wife persuaded her to go to the boat, and accompanied her. There was no one in the boat with her then. Abut 20 miantes afterwards as Mrs, Jackson and Tyrer's wife were standing at the rails overlooking the river, deceased was seen on the deck of their boat. She went sideways as if staggering, and • fell against the chimney of the boat which gave way, deceased falliug over the side of the boat and between the two boats. She never rose. Deceased was subse- quently get out of the water and two surgeons were sent for, but all efforts to rotor. life failed. Verdiot, "Accidentally downed."

div.p: LORD DUDLEY'S SEWAGE PROJECT.

At a meeting of the Dudley Town Council the mayor report )d that the Earl of Dudley had offered to take the whole of the sewerage from the drainage of Dudley on to his farm, free of expense, and to find an engineer to undertake the preparing for the sewerage scheme. div.head: JOHN BRIGHT.
div.p: JOHN BRIGHT.

ON Monday evening last a scene was enacted at the Manchester Reform Club which re- vived splendid memories in the minds of men who have passed the prime of life, while it stirred the pulses and invigorated the enthusiasm of the generation which is succeeding them. The noble dining hall of the club was filled by an audience, eager and keenly sympathetic, met to greet the greatest living orator, and to listen to his sagacious and high-minded counsels, un- folded in the fascinating eloquence of pure and simple w rds. Surrounded by men, themselves veterans of the great Liberal army, John Bright appeared like a general surrounded by his staff; one who, in spite of unnumbered victories and long service, re- sumes his armour and re-enters the fray, in his country's hour of need. The sad, ear- nest, thoughtful expression of a face be- longing to a physical type which is not generally associated with the highest forms of ideality; the dignified bearing of a man conscious of the responsibility of possessing powerful influence and the distinct and de- liberate utterance of a speaker whose thoughts are so clear to himself that he has time to pick his words as carefully as David picked the stones from the brook; these are the broad and tangible impressions of John Bright which you may bring away with you and communicate to another mind. Yet they would be so unjust to the man and would convey an impression so inadequate that you might as well attempt to interpret to the blind the countless beauties of cloud, colour, and sky in a landscape, by reading aloud a treatise on botany. it is not merely John Bright's words which are appealing to you, it is also his voice, his look, his gesture; it is not merely your ordinary self who is listening, for some of his enthusiasm is communicated to you, the finer sensibilities are awakened by the speaker and he prac- tises upon you like a mesmerist, who, once having secured your atten ion, places you under his influence and then does as he pleases until he voluntarily releases you. John Bright belongs to the rarest class of orators who at one and the' same time en- gage the mind, agitate the feelings, and charm the senses, and having thus com- pletely subjugated his hearers, he seems to rock them at his pleasure. (in Monday evening this power was peculiarly conspicu- ous, for the speech, alternating as it did between tenderness and indignation, yet not withqut its flashes of humour, and passages of lucid argument, excited every form of ex- pression which an audience can employ. Like a master playing upon an instrument, with a touch as light as it is firm, Mr. Bright evoked from the responsive crowd at his feet an unerring echo of all his great and gene- rous sentiments. It is needless to remark that the Eastern question being the paramount subject of the hour, going to hear Mr. Bright meant going to hear what the most sagacious and far-seeing statesman of the day would say on that perplexing subject. And as so much rubish has been talked and written by bewildered Tories at bay, about Liberals turning the Eastern question into a party question, it was wise on the part of Mr. Bright to follow Mr. Gladstone's lead in affirming that in one sense, and in one sense only, it is a party question. That Liberal politicians or the Liberal press have used the crisis like double-dealers, that they have sought to turn to account, for their own benefit, the generous enthusiasm awakened throughout the country, is untrue; nor is that calumny uttered by any but the un- scrupulous and the foolish. Lord Beacons- field. said as much at ,sylesbury, and one also hears it from people who know little more about politics than a Greenville Doc- tor of Philosophy knows about differential calculus or the Frogs of Arist _Thanes. It is true that a complexion of party spirit may be given to any public movement, by one side unanimously abstaining from taking part in it. ' A stranger visiting Warrington on the evening of the recent public meeting on the Bulgarian atrocities, and being told the political colour of the gentlemen who took part in the proceedings, might fairly have assumed, not that it was promoted to ad- vance. party interests, but that, at least, it had been convened to hear the views of Liberals only. 'Yet on that occasion it was really the local Tory party who turned the Eastern question into a party question; who shrank from their obvious publics duty as official chiefs of the community, and who were incapable, even in the very midst of the storm of popular emotion, of sinking their petty ,political personality. Yet, even if there were any grounds whatever for stating that a single responsible Liberal has endeavoued to make party capital out of the recent diplomatic failures of the foreign offic-e imagine, for one moment, the posidon of parties reversed, and think of the tre- mendous crushing things which Conserva- tives and parsons would have said of us by this time. We should have heard be.ore now that Mr. Gladstone had embraced the Mahometan creed, and had secretly paid a visit to the harem at Constantinople; that Mr. Lowe had made a fortune OD the Stock Exchange, by operating in Turkish bonds, and that Mr. Bright was solely engaged in shipping turbans at cost price to the insolvent firm on the Bosphorus. And yet this Bei- tern question is a party - question. It is naturally and inevitably a question with which only the Liberal party can deal in a manner to interpret satisfactorily the xvishes of a free people. When a party fights only for the perpetuation of existing things, it is fighting for the perpetuation of the evil as well as the good, and nee _ssarily for one class against another class; but when a party fights for freedom, progress, and equality of rights, it necessarily fights for all, wiihout distinction of race, creed, or country, Mr. Bright says ; "We devote the whole power of our party machinery not • • • • • • • to party but to general w al any- thing to extend political freedom it has been and d have public d o done objects, the freedom of all, as far as we could extend it. religious And Mr. Bright continues, "If under '-‘et, religious liberty has been in our auspi,... , . -"fled, no man's religious any manner extb_ "-hteet degree cur- liberty has been in the !sub_ crve sun- tailed. If by any measures we • _ ported, employment has been rendered moru constant and wages have beea raised, it has not been done or attempted to be done through the monopoly of law or the mono- poly of trade unions. It has been attempted to be done, and has been done, by measures broad and great, extending over the whole people, and whose beneficent action has been felt and, I hope, is now appreciated by all." And then he illustrates this text by pointing to the greater well-being of the people at this day, a condition of things which they owe to the Liberal legislation of the last 40 yeara, and which includes better food, better clothing, better shelter, and better education. in the sense then that our policy in the East FAMt WOlt 99;910t, 04491 A/

tion of even the semblance of partnership in the crimes of oppression, cruelty, and corrupt government, and that the inaugura- tion of that policy will assuredly have to ' come from the Liberal party—has indeed already come—this Eastern question is es- sentia ly a party question, that is to say a question for the Liberal party to determine, We will not follow Mr. Bright to the East, for every one has read his speiech and been touched by its tenderness, and impressed by its justice, and breadth of thought. No man is entitled to speak more authoritatively; indeed on this particular subject he might almost claim to be heard as a prophet. But in Mr. Bright there is little personal vanity, and it was in no jubilant tone, but in a voice of tender beseeching, that he told us some of the results of the Crimean war. To us, an immediate loss of 40 000 lives and one hun- dred millions of money. "Besides this," Mr. Bright says, "we entered into commer- cial transactions with an insosent firm on the Bosphorus, to whom the people of Eng- land advanced large sums which there is no hope they will ever see again—to the amount probably of nearly 100 millions sterling; and it may be said, looking back to those loans, that at this moment there is no iron- clad that slumbers on the Turkish waters, there is not a musket, or a rifle, or a bayonet, or a sword by which a Sarvian has bean killed in this war, or the unarmed men and the hapless women and children were mur- dered in Bulgaria, that was not purchased and paid for by money boirowed from the credulous people of this country. But dismissing the consideration of the Turkish question, excepting in the light of a question upon which we and our Govern- ment are at variance, Mr. Bright tells us, in no faltering words, what course we should take to bring about a reconciliation. We must use Avery legitimate me ins to compel the Prime Minister to meet Parliament, or to meet the constituencies at once. lie has defied the country; he has ridiculed the noblest popular rising since the time when the Duke of Wellington tried to form an anti-reform government, and he has failed to apprehend that the people of this country at this hour demand, and will soon insist upon, a policy in reference to Turkey diametrically opposed to that which Lord Derby has fortunately failed to carry out during the menacing and meaningless nego- tiations of the last six months. We do not expect Lord Beaconsfield to risk a dissolution of Parliament; that would, be suicide and not decapitation. But we, the people, have but to petition, in a voice loud enough and in tones not to be mistaken, for an autumn session; and if we succeed, one may safely hazard the prediction that the last words in Mr. Bright's speech would come true, "that we should have a solemn and irrevocable de- cision on the part of the people of this country—namely, that the blood and the treasure of England shall never again be wasted on behalf of the Turk, that the vote of our Government, the vote of England, in the parliament of Europe shall be given in favour of justice and freedom to Christian and Moslem alike, and that the Ottoman power shall be left hereafter to the fate which Providence has decreed to corruption, tyranny, and wrong."

The Berl of Carnarvon, Secretary of State for the Colonies, in dittributing the prizes to the scholars of the Derby Grammar School, on Monday, said he did n.t complain of the feeling which had been excited by the Bulgarian atrocities, and rejoiced to find that the hearts of his countrymen beat so soundly at such a tile of horrors. At the same time we must beware that no word and no act of ours jeopardised the peace of the world. A great war, it might be, at the present time hung in the balance, and at such a critical, al- most a supreme, moment it was not too much for the Governmeut to ask that patience should be exercised, and a fair and liberal construction given not only to their words, but still more to their intentions.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE IN THE NORTH.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE IN THE NORTH.

Replying to an address presented to him at Dunso, on Monday, Mr. Gladstone said we have arrived at a grave juncture, when it is secessary that the national mind should be expressed and respected. div.p: THANKS FOR MR. GLADSTONE.

Mr. Gladstone has received a telegram from Demetri Popovitz, the Mayor of Belgrade, thanking him, as the must powerful and eloquent statesman of free and Christian England, for having raised his voice and used his pen on behalf of oppressed Chriotians in the E ist. These resolutions were ordered by the meeting to be forwarded to Mr. Gladstone, and a select committee tyss also appointed to give fuller expression to the sentiments of the meet. ing in an address.

A TOWN'S MEETING. AT BIRMINGHAM. A letter from Mr. Bright was read at a town meeting held at Birmingham on Monday, for the purpose of calling upon the Queen to summon Parliament in order to consider the policy of the Government re. specting the Eastern Question. The right hon• gentleman expressed his opinion that an immediate assembling of Parliament, although All of moon. venience, was both contititational and wise. There were two ways out-of the existing difficulty—a com- plete reversal of our foreign policy as applied to the Eastern Question, or a resignation of the Liovernment. Mr. Pittuni a, M.P.. and Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., wore amongst the speakers, and a resolution affirming that the conditions of peace proposed by the Foreign Secre• tary were opposed to the wishes of the people, and that a petition be presented to the Queen praying her to immediately summon Parliament to consider the con- duct of the Government, was carried.
